What is research?

What is a human subject?

What makes research ethical?

---

After a quarter spent analyzing tools used to study society, in this session, we will ask about our obligations to society when using those tools.

* Was this *fabricating research*?
* Was this *unapproved human-subjects research*?

### Fabrication

Inventing research data or analytic results from scratch, and
distributing them in some way.

---

![Broockman, Kalla & Aronow (2015), "Irregularities in LaCour (2014)": the memo that exposed Michael LaCour's fabrication of data in a widely-cited Science study on persuasion and same-sex marriage attitudes.](images/lacour1.png)

---

![Finding #1: LaCour's "gay feeling thermometer" distribution is statistically identical to a national survey dataset he had access to — and different from all other reference datasets.](images/lacour2.png)

---

![Finding #4: respondents' feeling thermometer score changes are perfectly normally distributed — an implausibly clean pattern never seen in real survey data.](images/lacour3.png)

---

![Finding #8: all statistical irregularities in the data can be reproduced by a simple simulation starting from the 2012 CCAP dataset, consistent with the data having been fabricated rather than collected.](images/lacour4.png)

---

![R code from Broockman et al. demonstrating that adding small random noise to CCAP thermometer scores produces a distribution statistically indistinguishable from LaCour's claimed survey data.](images/lacour5.png)

---

![QQ plot: LaCour's Wave 3 data (x-axis) vs. simulated CCAP-based data (y-axis) fall almost perfectly on the diagonal. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test cannot distinguish them (p = 0.22), confirming the fabrication.](images/lacour6.png)

![Steven Lubet, "Ethics On The Run" (The New Rambler): a critical review of Alice Goffman's ethnography On the Run: Fugitive Life in an American City (2014).](images/goffman1.png)

---

![Lubet excerpt: Goffman describes police arresting men at a Philadelphia hospital maternity ward by checking patient lists, a claim Lubet finds implausible and sets out to verify.](images/goffman2.png)

---

![Lubet's challenge: even if police had the access Goffman describes, why would they prioritize a maternity ward over an emergency room for finding wanted individuals?](images/goffman3.png)

---

![A Philadelphia police source tells Lubet the hospital patient-list practice Goffman describes never existed: "No way. There was never any such policy or standard practice."](images/goffman4.png)

---

![Slate/The Atlantic: "The Ethics of Ethnography" (Neyfakh, 2015): Goffman's book draws fire for inconsistencies; the question is whether the author or the conventions of ethnography are to blame.](images/goffman5.png)

---

![Neyfakh's conclusion: Goffman's inaccuracies stem from ethnographic conventions requiring subject anonymity, and she changed details to protect identities, making the book "all but impossible to fact-check."](images/goffman6.png)

---

![Sociologists on the anonymity dilemma: "you don't even know if the people exist" (Winship) vs. "your honor is the only thing you have to make your stuff believable" (Taub); IRB anonymization requirements create an inherent verifiability problem.](images/goffman7.png)

---
### Questions to Consider

* Did Goffman do anything illegal?

* Did she violate sociological norms about researcher distance?

* Did her presence put her subjects at risk?

* Could she have studied the same question differently?

* What would you have done?

---

![Elman, Kapiszewski & Lupia, "Transparent Social Inquiry: Implications for Political Science" (Annual Review of Political Science).](images/transparency1.png)

---

![Table 1 from Elman et al.: a five-level typology of transparency (production, analytic, data access, production process, author contributor), with examples and DA-RT guidance at each level.](images/transparency2.png)

---
### Transparency in Practice

* Posting replication data and code

* Pre-registering study designs

* Disclosing funding sources

* Sharing materials for peer review

---

So, what makes research ethical?

* Institutional approval (IRB) is necessary but not sufficient

* Honesty in design, data collection, analysis, and reporting

* Respect for subjects' well-being and communities

* Transparency so others can build on your work

---

Ethics isn't a one-time checklist. It's about how we live our relationships with the communities of which we're part.

---
### A New Frontier: Using AI Tools in Research

Large language models are increasingly used in political science research — for coding open-ended survey responses, classifying news articles, analyzing social media text.

This raises ethical questions that IRBs don't cover and that the field hasn't fully resolved.

---
### Transparency Obligations

When you use an LLM as a measurement tool, the same transparency norms apply as with any other tool:

- **Report that you used it** — which model, which version, what prompt
- **Validate it** — show that its coding matches a human-coded gold standard on a sample
- **Report its limitations** — known biases, the stochastic nature of outputs (the same input can produce different outputs across runs)

LLM outputs are not deterministic. Treating a single run as a precise measurement misrepresents what you actually know.

This isn't a new ethical principle — it's the same obligation to honesty in data collection that applies to any instrument.

---
### An Unresolved Question: Training Data and Consent

LLMs are trained on vast quantities of text — including academic papers, books, and web content — typically without the knowledge or consent of the authors.

This raises a question the field hasn't answered: **Does using these tools make researchers complicit in that non-consensual appropriation?**

There is no settled answer. But it is the kind of ethical question that belongs in a researcher's self-reflection — not because IRBs require it, but because how we use tools shapes the systems we sustain.

---

So, what makes research ethical?

* Institutional approval (IRB) is necessary but not sufficient

* Honesty in design, data collection, analysis, and reporting

* Respect for subjects' well-being and communities

* Transparency so others can build on your work

* Awareness of the ethical dimensions of the tools we use
